plain_english:
It amazes me to watch people ask others for their time — and to see how easily others hand it over. Both sides think about the reason for the request, but neither one stops to consider the time itself. As if asking for someone's time were asking for nothing. As if giving it away were giving up nothing.

We treat time like a toy, even though it is the most valuable thing we have. But because you can't hold it in your hands or see it with your eyes, people think it's cheap. Most put almost no value on it at all.

People will guard their money fiercely. They'll rent out their labor, their expertise, their attention — all to earn more of it. But time? They give that away for free, as though it costs them nothing.
original_excerpt: I am filled with wonder when I see some men asking others for their time, and those who are asked for it most willing to give it: both parties consider the object for which the time is given, but neither of them thinks of the time itself, as though in asking for this one asked for nothing, and in giving it one gave nothing: we play with what is the most precious of all things: yet it escapes men's notice, because it is an incorporeal thing, and because it does not come before our eyes; and therefore it is held very cheap, nay, hardly any value whatever is put upon it. Men set the greatest store upon presents or pensions, and hire out their work, their services, or their care in order to gain them: no one values time: they give it much more freely, as though it cost nothing.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 8

plain_english:
And yet, these same people — when they get sick and death feels close — will beg their doctors on their knees to save them. If they're facing execution, they'll give up everything they own just to keep living. The contradiction is stunning.

Imagine if everyone could see exactly how many years they had left, the way we can count the years already behind us. People with only a few years remaining would guard every moment. But here's the thing: it's easy to budget a small amount when you know the total. What you really need to protect is the thing that could run out at any time — and you have no idea when that will be.
original_excerpt: Yet you will see these same people clasping the knees of their physician as suppliants when they are sick and in present peril of death, and if threatened with a capital charge willing to give all that they possess in order that they may live: so inconsistent are they. Indeed, if the number of every man's future years could be laid before him, as we can lay that of his past years, how anxious those who found that they had but few years remaining would be to make the most of them? Yet it is easy to arrange the distribution of a quantity, however small, if we know how much there is: what you ought to husband most carefully is that which may run short you know not when.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 8

plain_english:
Still, don't think people don't know how precious time is. They love to tell the people closest to them, "I'd give you some of my own years." And they do give them — without realizing it. But they give them in a way where they lose the time themselves and the other person never actually gains it. They don't see where their supply is coming from, so they can tolerate wasting what they can't see.

But no one will give you back your years. No one will return them to you. Once your life has started moving, it keeps going. It will not start over or undo what it has done. It won't make a sound. It won't warn you how fast it's flying by. It will glide along in silence. It won't slow down for a king's command or a whole nation's wish. However it began on its first day, that's how it will continue — never turning aside, never pausing.

So what follows from all this? You're busy. But life is rushing past you. Death will show up eventually, and you will have to deal with him — whether you want to or not.
original_excerpt: Yet you have no reason to suppose that they do not know how dear a thing time is: they are wont to say to those whom they especially love that they are ready to give them a part of their own years. They do give them, and know not that they are giving them; but they give them in such a manner that they themselves lose them without the others gaining them. They do not, however, know whence they obtain their supply, and therefore they are able to endure the waste of what is not seen: yet no one will give you back your years, no one will restore them to you again: your life will run its course when once it has begun, and will neither begin again or efface what it has done. It will make no disturbance, it will give you no warning of how fast it flies: it will move silently on: it will not prolong itself at the command of a king, or at the wish of a nation: as it started on its first day, so it will run: it will never turn aside, never delay. What follows, then? Why! you are busy, but life is hurrying on: death will be here some time or other, and you must attend to him, whether you will or no.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 8
